newsitem.title: FRANCE: Veteran French Africa kingmaker Foccart dies at 83.
newsitem.headline: Veteran French Africa kingmaker Foccart dies at 83.

text.p: Veteran French Africa kingmaker Jacques Foccart, who pulled strings on the continent for three presidents and was General de Gaulle's spymaster, died at his Paris home on Wednesday, an aide said. He was 83.
"We found him dead at the end of the night. I think it was heart failure," his aide Fernand Wibaux said from Foccart's home.
Foccart, who returned to the Elysee palace in 1995 as an honorary adviser to President Jacques Chirac, had long been ill with Parkinson's disease and had not left his home for months.

His death came at a moment of crisis in France's Africa policy, with one of Paris' longest-serving proteges, Zaire strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, in hospital in Monaco for cancer treatment while rebels sweep across the east of his country.

As secretary-general for African affairs at the presidency from 1958 to 1974, and later without any official role, Foccart controlled a network of agents across Africa for nearly 40 years, making and breaking regimes to serve French political and commercial interests.

But Foccart was as famous for his secret service links. These began in the wartime anti-Nazi resistance and culminated with the creation of "les barbouzes" ("the beards"), undercover agents who waged counter-terror against French extremists in Algeria in 1961-62 at the end of the war of independence.
Foccart published a first volume of memoirs in 1995 that left many gaps in his cloak-and-dagger career.
Press reports said he had deferred publication of a second volume on politics and intelligence work until after his death because it contained such explosive revelations.
Rarely seen in public, the bald, round-headed, bespectacled Foccart was once described as the "most secret man in France".

He owed his career to General de Gaulle and, in a rare television appearance, admitted his greatest disappointment was the general's refusal to meet him after he stayed on as an adviser to Georges Pompidou, de Gaulle's successor in 1969.
Foccart long wielded power in the Gaullist political party, where he was known as one of the inner circle of "barons."
"A great servant of our country has disappeared," said Economic Cooperation Minister Jacques Gofrain said in a tribute.
"He devoted his life to the emancipation of thousands...and was faithful to the action and thoughts of General de Gaulle."

Always a controversial figure, Foccart was accused of ordering murders and was a target of smear campaigns. Friends said one was launched by U.S. intelligence when De Gaulle distanced himself from Washington in the early 1960s.

Foccart launched the first of a long series of French military interventions in Africa in 1964 in Gabon to reinstate an ousted president. At one time, a dozen African heads of state were said to owe their positions to his intrigues.
More recently, he was accused of pursuing a parallel African policy in support of old French cronies that contradicted Paris' official support for economic and democratic reform.
Critics said Foccart's networks were used to recycle French aid money to fund the Gaullist party back home.
Symbolically, Chirac took the veteran Gaullist "Mr Africa" along on his first trip to the continent as president in 1995.
But French policymakers complain that Foccart's role was more than symbolic.

They said two Africa policies co-exist uneasily in Chirac's office -- an official one run by former ambassador Michel Dupuch and a "kitchen cabinet" run by Foccart and Wibaux, which keeps its own contacts and sometimes countermands official policy.
